summary.text: Plant hormones are signal molecules produced within plants that occur in extremely low concentrations.
They control all aspects of plant growth and development, including embryogenesis, organ size, pathogen defense, stress tolerance and reproductive development.
Unlike in animals, where hormone production is restricted to specialized glands, each plant cell is capable of producing hormones.

facts.label: Term coined by
facts.value: Went and Thimann, in their 1937 book

facts.label: First five classes
facts.value: Abscisic acid, auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and ethylene

facts.label: Later additions
facts.value: Brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid and strigolactones

facts.label: Not nutrients
facts.value: They influence growth and development in small amounts

items.prompt: Animals make hormones in specialised glands. Where would you look for the glands in a plant?

options.label: In the roots only
In the leaves, which hold the glands
There are none; each cell can produce hormones
In the phloem, which stores them all

items.explain: Plants lack glands to produce and store hormones; each plant cell is capable of producing them.

items.prompt: A pinch of plant hormone changes how a seedling grows, but adding more does not feed it. Why?

options.label: Hormones are signals that influence growth in small amounts, not nutrients
Hormones are nutrients that are only used in tiny doses
Seedlings cannot absorb anything through their leaves
Hormones are stored in glands until the seedling is older

items.explain: Plant hormones are not nutrients, but chemicals that in small amounts promote and influence growth, development and differentiation.

items.prompt: A hormone must reach a spot far from where it was made, such as from the leaves to the roots. What carries it?

options.label: Cytoplasmic streaming inside each cell
A lymph system like the one animals have
Slow diffusion between neighbouring cells
Vascular tissues such as the phloem and xylem

items.explain: Cytoplasmic streaming and slow diffusion handle local movement, while vascular tissues move hormones from one part of the plant to another.

items.prompt: A hormone reaches a whole shoot, but only some cells react, and only at certain times in their lives. Why?

options.label: Only cells beside a vein can detect it
Only some cells respond, at specific points in their growth cycle
Cells respond equally throughout their lives
The hormone breaks down before it reaches most cells

items.explain: Not all plant cells respond to hormones; those that do are programmed to respond at specific points in their growth cycle.

items.prompt: How can a plant switch off a hormone it no longer needs?

options.label: It can inactivate the hormone or break it down chemically
It sends it out through the stomata
It cannot, as the effect lasts for the cell's life
It lets the xylem flush it into the soil

items.explain: Plants can inactivate hormones, conjugate them, or break them down chemically, effectively destroying them.

items.prompt: Auxins and cytokinins applied together boost cell division more than either does alone. What is this interaction called?

options.label: Conjugation
Differentiation
Synergism
Gene expression

items.explain: Synergism means two or more hormones together have an effect greater than their individual effects, as auxins and cytokinins do for cell proliferation.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical signals
paragraphs.text: Plant hormones, also called phytohormones, are signal molecules that plants make themselves and that are present at extremely low levels. They are not nutrients. Instead, in small amounts they promote and shape the growth, development and specialisation of cells and tissues. They control every side of a plant's growth, from the embryo and the size of its organs to fighting disease, tolerating stress and reproducing.

paragraphs.heading: No glands needed
paragraphs.text: In animals, hormones come only from special glands, but in plants every cell can make them. Plants have no glands to make or store hormones, and rather than the two circulatory systems animals have, they move chemicals around by more passive means. They use simple chemicals as hormones, which pass easily through their tissues and are often made and used close by. Hormones are very often made at sites of active growth in the meristems, before cells have fully specialised.

paragraphs.heading: Getting around the plant
paragraphs.text: Hormones travel through the plant in four ways. Over short distances, cytoplasm streams within cells and molecules diffuse slowly between cells. Over long distances, they ride in the vascular tissues: the phloem, which takes sugars from leaves to roots and flowers, and the xylem, which carries water and minerals from the roots to the foliage. Once made, a hormone may be sent elsewhere to act at once, or stored in cells for later release.

paragraphs.heading: Turning signals up and down
paragraphs.text: Not every plant cell responds to hormones, and those that do respond at set points in their growth. Plants also need to switch a hormone's effects off when it is no longer needed. They can limit the raw chemicals used to build hormones, store hormones, inactivate them, or bind them to carbohydrates, amino acids or peptides. They can also break hormones down, dilute them by moving them about, and use one hormone to adjust the levels of another.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to study
paragraphs.text: Plants respond to hormone levels of only 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵ mol/L. Such tiny amounts made hormones very hard to study, and scientists only began to piece together their roles in the late 1970s. The first scientific observations date to the 1880s, and identifying the hormones took another 70 years. Early researchers studied plants that genetically lacked a hormone, or grew plants in culture with different hormone mixes and compared the results.

paragraphs.heading: The main families
paragraphs.text: Early research named five major classes: auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and ethylene. Brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid and strigolactones were later added to that list. Abscisic acid is one of the most important growth inhibitors. Hormones can also act in synergy, meaning two or more together have a bigger effect than each alone. Auxins and cytokinins, for example, together boost cell division and organ formation more than either can by itself.
